_ghi_chu: EN-ALL GĐ 2 — bản phủ tiếng Anh của từ điển thuật ngữ (tu_dien.json). Ban biên tập viết từ nghĩa; tên theo thuat_ngu_en.json / ten_en.json.
_nguon: Plain-English glossary of Zi Wei Dou Shu, BaZi, Feng Shui, I Ching and numerology terms. Written by the editorial team; drafts awaiting native-speaker review.

muc.de_hieu: A map of 12 boxes (12 palaces) drawn from the hour, day, month and year of your birth in the lunar calendar. Each box is one area of life and holds 'stars' — old symbols that describe how that area tends to go.
muc.vi_du: Like the floor plan of a house with 12 rooms, each room holding different furniture (stars).

muc.de_hieu: One of the 12 boxes of the chart. Each box stands for one area of life: yourself, siblings, spouse, children, money, health, travel, friends, career, home, inner life and parents.
The most important box. It is about you: your basic character and how you respond to life. Reading a chart always starts here.
The palace that shows which area of life you put your energy into in the second half of life. 'Body Palace in the Career Palace' means that later on you put great weight on your career.
The palace covering your brothers and sisters, and close friends of your own age.
The palace covering love, marriage and the kind of person you easily bond with.
The palace covering your children, your students and younger people you look after.
The palace covering how you earn, keep and spend money.
The palace covering your body and the parts of it worth keeping an eye on. It is not for diagnosing illness and it is not medical advice — for any health concern, see a doctor.
The palace covering the times you step out into society, travel far or work in an unfamiliar setting.
The palace covering friends, colleagues and people who work under you — people on your level or below.
The palace covering your work and profession, how you work and how you move up.
The palace covering your home, land and property, and the atmosphere in your family.
The palace covering your inner life, the joy you feel inside, and the blessings that come down through your family line.
The palace covering your parents, your mentors and how you get on with people above you.

When you read one palace, you also look at 3 other palaces that 'shine' on it: the two that form a triangle with it (the three harmonies) and the one directly opposite. Together these four palaces shape one area of life.
muc.vi_du: To read the Life Palace, you also look at the Wealth Palace and the Career Palace (the triangle) and the Travel Palace (opposite).

muc.de_hieu: The 14 main stars, which set the 'character' of each palace. The other stars only add colour.
The secondary stars that sit next to a major star, either adding help (auspicious stars) or causing obstacles (malefic stars).
A palace with no major star in it. You then borrow the stars of the opposite palace to read it. People whose Life Palace is an empty palace tend to be flexible and shaped by their surroundings.
A number (2–6) tied to one of the five elements and worked out from the Life Palace. It decides where the Zi Wei star sits and the age at which your first Major Period begins.
muc.vi_du: Earth Five Bureau: the first Major Period starts at age 5.

muc.de_hieu: The star that 'stands for' your basic self, set by the Earthly Branch of your birth year — a minor reference point.
The star that 'stands for' the Body Palace, set by your birth year — a minor reference point.

The 'poetic' element tied to the stem-and-branch pair of your birth year, such as 'Lu Pang Tu' (Earth by the Roadside). In everyday talk people often call it your 'element', as in 'people born this year are Metal'.
muc.vi_du: Geng Wu (1990) is Lu Pang Tu (Earth by the Roadside).

muc.de_hieu: Whether your birth year has a yang or a yin stem, combined with your sex, decides the direction of each Major Period and of some stars (forward or backward).
The palace whose stem matches the stem of your birth year — a side technique of the Flying Star school of Zi Wei. The site only notes it and does not use it for the main reading.
Each star is 'strong' or 'weak' depending on the palace it sits in — like a plant that does or does not suit its soil. The levels are Temple, Prosperous, Favourable, Neutral and Fallen.
The brightest level: the star sits in its proper 'home' and shows its good side most clearly.
Fairly strong; its good side is easy to see.
The star sits in a suitable place and works fairly well.
An average level; good or bad depends on the stars beside it.
The star sits in an unsuitable place, so its harder side shows more easily. This does not mean 'bad' — only that you need more effort and more self-awareness.

The way of reading Zi Wei found in Vietnamese books (Thai Thu Lang, Nguyen Phat Loc…). It differs from the Chinese schools in a few lookup tables, such as star brightness and how the Huo Xing and Ling Xing stars are placed.
A Chinese school of Zi Wei. The star placement the site uses follows this school; the site marks clearly where it differs from Vietnamese books and lets you choose.
Four 'transformations' attached to 4 stars according to the stem of your birth year: Hua Lu, Hua Quan, Hua Ke and Hua Ji — like 4 labels that make a star stand out in one direction.
The label for 'gain and smooth flow': an area with Hua Lu usually goes well and tends to bring a harvest.
The label for 'holding power and taking charge': in that area you want to decide for yourself, and you have influence.
The label for 'reputation and learning': in that area you are easily recognised, and helpful people lift you up.
The label for 'snags and worry': that area easily weighs on your mind and calls for care — it is also the place you care about most.
A 'gap' mark placed between two palaces according to your birth year. It weakens the stars inside at first, and they only show clearly later. Difficult stars that meet the Xun Void become less harsh.
A 'roadblock' mark between two palaces according to the stem of your birth year. It holds things back strongly in the early part of life (usually before age 30).

A named 'combination of stars' described in old books, such as the Zi-Fu-Wu-Xiang group or the Sha-Po-Lang group. A chart pattern is only a reference frame — whether it works out still depends on the difficult stars that come with it.
When a good chart pattern meets difficult stars (Qing Yang, Tuo Luo, Huo Xing, Ling Xing, Di Kong, Di Jie, Hua Ji) that weaken its good meaning.
Six stars that cause obstacles: Qing Yang, Tuo Luo, Huo Xing, Ling Xing, Di Kong and Di Jie. They make life more testing, but they also give you the push to bounce back.
Six helpful stars: Zuo Fu, You Bi, Wen Chang, Wen Qu, Tian Kui and Tian Yue — like having people who help you, a way with words, and benefactors.
A 10-year stage of life, each stage tied to one palace. When you read the timing of a chart, always look at the Major Period first.
muc.vi_du: A Major Period from 25–34 in the Career Palace: for these ten years, work is the centre of attention.

muc.de_hieu: The year-by-year period by age, moving through the 12 palaces — a secondary layer under the Major Period and the annual flow.
The influence of one particular solar or lunar year (by the year's Earthly Branch), laid on top of your birth chart to see which areas stand out that year.

muc.ten: East Asian age (counted from birth as 1)
muc.de_hieu: The Vietnamese way of counting age: you are already 1 at birth and add 1 at each Lunar New Year (Tet). Zi Wei periods are counted by this East Asian age.
Born between 23:00 and 23:59. Zi Wei treats this as already the next day, while numerology and BaZi keep it as the same day — so the site always adds a note for people born at this hour.
A lunar month 'slotted in' so the calendar stays in step with the seasons. For people born in the second half of a leap month there are two ways to set up the chart — the site shows you both.
The 'emperor' star: self-respecting, likes to lead, has presence. Worth watching: can become proud and dislikes hearing other views.
The 'advisor' star: quick-witted, good at planning, enjoys change. Worth watching: tends to overthink and finds it hard to stay with one thing.
The 'sun' star: giving, warm-hearted, likes to be recognised. Worth watching: takes on other people's work and wears itself out easily.
The 'finance' star: practical, decisive, good with money. Worth watching: rigid, rarely shows its feelings.
The 'kind-hearted' star: gentle, easy-going, likes an easy life. Worth watching: lacks drive and tends to put things off.
The 'principles' star: firm views, strong, passionate. Worth watching: can go to extremes and clash with others.
The 'storehouse' star: steady, good at keeping what it has, thoughtful. Worth watching: overly cautious, shies away from risk.
The 'moon' star: subtle, full of feeling, cares for the family. Worth watching: tends to keep private worries to itself.
The 'many talents, many wants' star: good at socialising, many interests. Worth watching: easily scattered, fond of fun.
The 'speech' star: good at analysis and debate. Worth watching: draws gossip easily, and blunt words can cause offence.
The 'seal of office' star: trustworthy, fair, likes helping others. Worth watching: easily pulled into other people's affairs.
The 'protector' star: chivalrous, like an eldest brother, suited to teaching and caring work. Worth watching: tends to lecture and can be stubborn.
The 'vanguard general' star: brave, willing to take on hard jobs. Worth watching: impatient, prone to taking risks.
The 'tear down the old, build the new' star: loves renewal and does not mind knocking things down to start again. Worth watching: unpredictable, wasteful of resources.
The 'helper on the left' star: you have people to help you and you work well in a team.
The 'helper on the right' star: you have backing and are good at working with others.
The 'letters' star: good at study and writing; paperwork goes smoothly.
The 'artistic talent' star: a way with words, the arts, skill and tact.
The 'daytime benefactor' star: you meet good people who help you openly.
The 'night-time benefactor' star: help comes to you quietly, behind the scenes.
The 'savings' star: keeps money well and builds up slowly but surely.
The 'heavenly horse' star: travel, change, energy. When it meets Lu (prosperity), money comes easily through moving around.
A malefic star, the 'spear': forceful, competitive, prone to head-on clashes.
A malefic star of 'tangles': delays, drawn-out matters, things that drag on.
A malefic star of 'flaring fire': hot-tempered and sudden, quick to come and quick to go.
A malefic star of 'smouldering fire': frustration held inside, hidden pressure.
A malefic star of 'emptiness': unusual ideas, but easy disappointment and losses.
A malefic star of 'loss': sudden upheavals, so keep something in reserve.
The 'red thread' star: love, weddings, charm.
The 'joy' star: happy events, parties, good news.
The 'peach blossom' star: attractiveness and appeal to the opposite sex.
The 'discipline and law' star: strict, suited to law, the military and medicine; it also points to gossip and disputes.
The 'romantic' star: romantic, artistic, easily caught up in love affairs.
The 'tears' star: sorrow, but also depth.
The 'drain' star: worry and a feeling of emptiness.
The 'big spending' star: heavy spending, material loss.
The 'small spending' star: petty expenses, things slipping away.
The 'stairs' star: status, moving up step by step.
The 'seat' star: position and stability.
The 'favour' star: receiving favours and praise.
The 'noble' star: being respected, having benefactors.
The 'dragon pool' star: talent and good fortune in writing and the arts.
The 'phoenix pavilion' star: style, elegance, a good name.
The 'lonely' star (for men): likes independence, shares little.
The 'solitary' star (for women): an inward life, independent.

A cycle of 12 stages, like the life of a tree: Growth (Chang Sheng), Bath, Youth, Prime, Peak, Decline, Sickness, Death, Grave, Extinction, Conception, Nurture. It shows how much vitality each palace has.
A cycle of 12 stars set by the Earthly Branch of your birth year, about your attitude to life and your social relationships.
A cycle of 12 stars that starts from Lu Cun, about wealth and smaller career gains.
A group of 4 'management and stability' stars meeting on the Life Palace: suited to organising, finance and administration.
A group of 3 'change and daring' stars meeting on the Life Palace: a life with many changes, suited to starting a business and to competition.
A group of 4 'gentle, specialist' stars meeting on the Life Palace: suited to stable jobs, office work, expert roles and service.
Ju Men and Tai Yang in the same palace or facing each other: your words carry weight, suited to teaching, media and diplomacy.
Eight characters that record the hour, day, month and year of birth. Each one is a pair of a Heavenly Stem and an Earthly Branch, called a 'pillar'. Four pillars = eight characters.
muc.vi_du: Geng Wu · Xin Si · Ren Wu · Bing Wu

muc.de_hieu: A column made of 1 stem + 1 branch. The Year Pillar relates to your roots, the Month Pillar to the setting you grew up in, the Day Pillar to yourself and your spouse, and the Hour Pillar to your children and later life.
10 symbols — Jia, Yi, Bing, Ding, Wu, Ji, Geng, Xin, Ren, Gui — each carrying one element (Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal, Water) and being either yin or yang.
12 symbols — Zi, Chou, Yin… Hai (the 12 zodiac animals) — used for the year, month, day and hour.
The stem of the Day Pillar — it stands for you. Everything else in BaZi is read in relation to this character.
muc.vi_du: Born on a Ren Wu day → Day Master Ren (great water).

muc.de_hieu: Five kinds of 'qi': Metal, Wood, Water, Fire and Earth. They produce and control one another in a cycle.
muc.vi_du: Wood produces Fire (wood feeds a fire); Water controls Fire (water puts out fire).

muc.de_hieu: Each element nourishes the next: Wood → Fire → Earth → Metal → Water → Wood.
Each element keeps another in check: Wood controls Earth, Earth controls Water, Water controls Fire, Fire controls Metal, Metal controls Wood.
The stems 'hidden' inside each Earthly Branch. For example, the branch Si hides Bing, Geng and Wu. They are the quiet strength of the chart.
When a stem hidden in a branch also shows up in the row of stems above — that strength has 'come out' and is easy to use.
The Earthly Branch of your birth month — the 'season' you were born in, which decides which element is strong. It is the most important character for setting the chart pattern.
Ten 'roles' the other stems play in relation to the Day Master (you): like a sibling, a creative child, money, a boss, a protector…
On an equal footing — the same element and the same yin/yang as you: friends, siblings, a spirit of independence.
The same element but the opposite yin/yang: a rival, but also the strength to compete for what you want.
What you produce in a relaxed way: talent, enjoyment, gentle creativity.
What you produce in a sharp way: unconventional creativity, a gift for speech, the nerve to push against the rules.
Steady money and honest work; for a man it also stands for the wife.
Unexpected money, opportunities, business; also the father.
Rules and order, the boss, honour; for a woman it also stands for the husband.
Pressure, challenges and tough authority — both a strain and a driving force.
Protection, education, the mother, the people who support you.
Knowledge of your own, an original way of thinking, protection that comes in unusual ways.
The Day Master (you) has many elements of the same kind, or elements that feed it — plenty of energy that needs an outlet to 'flow out' into.
The Day Master gets little support — it needs nourishing and building up.
The element 'you need' to balance the chart. The site sets out two ways of finding it (the support-and-restrain method and the climate-adjusting method) and does not choose for you.
A way of finding the Useful God by the rule 'if it is weak, build it up; if it is strong, drain it' for the Day Master.
A way of finding the Useful God from the climate of your birth season: born in a hot season, you need water; born in a cold season, you need fire.
An element or factor that helps, making the chart work better.
An element or factor that works against you, throwing the chart off balance.
A 10-year stage in BaZi. Each stage brings a new stem-and-branch pair that acts on the chart.
Two 'empty' branches set by the Day Pillar — that spot is left open, as it were, and matters linked to it easily come to nothing.
The 'minor stars' of BaZi, such as the Heavenly Noble, Peach Blossom and Travelling Horse — side signals, not part of the main reading.
The best of the symbolic stars: someone helps you when times are hard.
The Shen Sha (symbolic star) of movement, moving house and working far away.
The extreme strength of a yang Day Master — decisive, but prone to going too far.
The birth month is where the Day Master 'has its prosperity' — self-reliant, standing firm on its own strength.
An Earthly Branch pair that 'shakes hands', such as Zi–Chou or Yin–Hai: connection and harmony.
An Earthly Branch pair that faces off, such as Zi–Wu: clashes, change, upheaval.
Three branches that combine into one strong element group, such as Shen–Zi–Chen forming Water.
A 'hurting' relationship between branches — prone to worry and gossip.
24 climate markers in the year, set by the position of the sun (Start of Spring, Awakening of Insects…). BaZi changes month at the solar term, not on the 1st day of the lunar month.
The first solar term of the year (around 4 February, early in month 2 of the solar calendar). BaZi and Feng Shui change year at the Start of Spring, not at Lunar New Year (Tet).
A classic book from the Qing dynasty on balancing the climate for each Day Master born in each month (the climate-adjusting method of finding the Useful God).
A classic book from the Qing dynasty (by Shen Xiaozhan) on setting the BaZi chart pattern by birth month.
A figure of 6 stacked lines, each either solid (yang) or broken (yin). There are 64 hexagrams, and each one describes a 'situation' a matter is in.
One of the 6 lines of a hexagram, counted from the bottom up: line 1 is the beginning, line 6 is the end or peak.
A solid line —, standing for strength, initiative and light.
A broken line - -, standing for softness, receptiveness and stillness.
A line that is 'turning' into its opposite (solid to broken, or the other way round) — the key point of what you are asking about.
The hexagram you cast — the present situation.
The hexagram you get when each changing line flips — the direction the matter is moving in.
The hexagram built from the middle lines — how things develop on the inside, the 'hidden' part.
8 figures of 3 lines: Qian (heaven), Kun (earth), Zhen (thunder), Xun (wind), Kan (water), Li (fire), Gen (mountain), Dui (lake). Two trigrams stacked together make 1 of the 64 hexagrams.
The top three lines of a hexagram — the outside world, other people.
The bottom three lines — the inside, you yourself.
The ancient words on the whole hexagram, e.g. 'origin, success, benefit, steadfastness' for Qian.
The ancient words about each line on its own — read when that line is changing.
The part of the Ten Wings (the commentaries of the Confucian school) that explains the Judgment.
The 'image' commentary on a hexagram, with advice for the noble person, such as 'Heaven moves with strength; the noble person keeps strengthening themselves without rest'.
The four virtues of the Qian hexagram: a great beginning, flowing through, benefit, and holding firm to what is right. Put simply: things go well if you do them rightly and keep at it.
Something to regret, but it can still be put right if you know when to stop and adjust.
Difficulty, a small dead end, or something to feel ashamed of — caused by stubbornness or hesitation.
Good and favourable — the matter is on the right track if you keep doing it this way.
Bad, with risk — a reminder to be careful, change your approach or wait for the right time.
No fault — acting this way is fine and brings no blame.
A way of reading hexagrams through their moral meaning and their advice on how to conduct yourself (Wang Bi, Cheng Yi, Zhu Xi).
A way of reading a hexagram by attaching stems and branches to its 6 lines and weighing how they produce and control one another, to judge a specific matter (the book Zeng Shan Bu Yi).
A way of setting up a hexagram from numbers, the time, or things you happen to come across, traditionally credited to Shao Yong of the Song dynasty.
In Six Lines divination: the line that stands for the person asking.
In Six Lines divination: the line that stands for the other party, or the other side of the matter.
Five roles attached to the lines in Six Lines divination: Parents (papers, protection), Siblings (competition), Offspring (cheerfulness, relief), Wealth (money) and Officer Ghost (work, pressure).
The line that stands for what you are asking about — for money look at Wealth, for work look at Officer Ghost, for papers look at Parents.
The Earthly Branch of the month when casting a hexagram — used to judge which lines are strong and which are weak.
The Earthly Branch of the day when casting a hexagram — also used to judge the strength of the lines.
How a hexagram is set up: toss 3 coins 6 times (each toss gives one line), or use numbers or the time. The site can cast at random for you, or you cast it yourself and enter the result.
Your personal trigram in Eight Mansions, worked out from your birth year and sex. It places you in the East group or the West group.
The group whose Kua number falls on Kan, Li, Zhen or Xun — suited to the North, South, East and South-East directions.
The group whose Kua number falls on Qian, Kun, Gen or Dui — suited to North-West, South-West, North-East and West.
A Feng Shui school that sorts the 8 directions into 4 good and 4 bad ones according to the Kua number of the person living there.
Eight 'qualities' each direction has for each Kua number: 4 good (Sheng Qi, Tian Yi, Yan Nian, Fu Wei) and 4 bad (Jue Ming, Wu Gui, Liu Sha, Huo Hai).
The best direction: vitality, growth, wealth.
A good direction for health and for getting help.
A good direction for relationships and a lasting marriage.
A calm, stable direction, good for study and a quiet mind.
The worst direction in Eight Mansions: prone to loss and drain, so avoid having the main door, the bed or the stove face it.
A bad direction: prone to gossip, trouble and things going missing.
A bad direction: trouble in love, lawsuits, small problems.
A mildly bad direction: annoyances and tiredness.
The 'back' of the house — opposite the direction its front faces.
The direction the front of the house looks out toward.
The compass divides 360° into 24 parts of 15° each, named after stems, branches and trigrams (Ren, Zi, Gui, Chou…).
A Feng Shui school that looks at 'flying stars' over time: every 20 years (one Period), the numbers 1–9 move through the 9 squares of the house.
A 20-year cycle in Xuan Kong. We are now in Period 9 (2024–2043), when star number 9 is 'prosperous'.
The nine 'stars' numbered 1–9 in Xuan Kong, each with its own colour and nature (e.g. 1 White, 5 Yellow, 9 Purple).
The Period number placed in each square — the 'background' of that era.
The number on the left of each square: about people, health and relationships — best placed in a quiet spot with a 'mountain' (a wall, tall furniture).
The number on the right of each square: about money and opportunity — best placed in an open spot with 'water' (a door, a walkway).
The usual way of setting up a Xuan Kong chart, when the house sits exactly in the centre of one mountain.
The chart used when the house is more than 3° off the centre of a mountain (a mixed facing): the middle number is swapped for a 'replacement star' by the traditional formula.
The best chart: the prosperous star is at both the back of the house (people) and the front (money).

muc.ten: Reversed (Up the Mountain, Down the Water)
bien_the: Up the Mountain, Down the Water
muc.de_hieu: A reversed chart: the people star runs to the front of the house and the money star runs to the back — the layout needs to make up for it.
Both prosperous stars sit at the front of the house: good for money, but keep an eye on matters of people.
Both prosperous stars sit at the back of the house: good for people; keep the back open to stir up money.
A number that matches the base number of its square — like 'marking time', stagnation.
A number that adds up to 10 with the base number of its square — like a 'reversal', upheaval.
The year's numbers flying into the squares — in 2026, star number 1 (White) sits in the centre. The year changes at the Start of Spring.
A facing that falls right on the boundary between two mountains — the energy is mixed, so measure again.
The most important number, added up from your day, month and year of birth. It is about your path and the main lessons of your life.
The number from all the letters of your full name — your talents and how you show yourself to the world.
The number from the vowels in your name — what you truly long for inside.
The number from the consonants in your name — the first impression other people get of you.
The numbers 11, 22 and 33, which are not reduced any further — they carry strong energy and greater pressure.
A number in a 9-year cycle, based on your birth date and the current year — the theme of that year for you personally.
The smaller theme of each month within your Personal Year.
Four big stages of life, each with its own theme number and age range.
Numbers that point to the hard lessons you tend to meet again in each stage.
The numbers 13, 14, 16 and 19 that appear while adding up — they hint at a lesson to correct from old habits (according to numerology).
A 3×3 grid that places the digits of your birth date in squares 1–9, so you can see which numbers appear often and which are missing.
A straight row of 3 squares on the Birth Date Grid that are all filled (an arrow of strength) or all empty (an empty arrow) — it points to a standout personality trait.

The most widely used way of working out numerology in Vietnam: each letter matches a number from 1 to 9 in alphabetical order; you add up the birth date and full name, then reduce. It has the Master Numbers 11, 22 and 33.
muc.vi_du: A is 1, B is 2 … I is 9, then J is 1 again.

muc.de_hieu: An older way of working out numerology. It gives letters the numbers 1 to 8 by how they sound (there is no 9), puts weight on the name you are usually called, and uses compound numbers from 10 to 52.
muc.vi_du: The same name can give two different numbers in the Pythagorean and Chaldean systems — two viewpoints, not one right and one wrong.

muc.de_hieu: A two-digit number before it is reduced (for example 23 before it adds up to 5). The Chaldean school reads the meaning of compound numbers on their own, alongside the root number.
The shared name for Direct Wealth and Indirect Wealth — the element the Day Master controls. In BaZi, the Wealth star is about money and possessions, and for men it is also linked to the wife.
muc.vi_du: If the Day Master is Wood, the Wealth star is Earth (Wood controls Earth).

muc.de_hieu: The shared name for Direct Officer and Seven Killings — the element that controls the Day Master. It is about discipline, bosses and work with rules; for women it is also linked to the husband.
muc.vi_du: If the Day Master is Water, the Officer star is Earth (Earth controls Water).

muc.de_hieu: The shared name for Direct Resource and Indirect Resource — the element that produces the Day Master. It is about study, protection, people who support you, and paperwork.
muc.vi_du: If the Day Master is Fire, the Resource star is Wood (Wood produces Fire).

muc.de_hieu: The age at which you enter your first Luck Pillar, counted from your birthday to the nearest solar term (three days count as one year). Before that age, the chart is read through the Month Pillar.

The stem and branch of each year (counted from the Start of Spring), set beside the four pillars to see how that year affects the Day Master: if it adds strength to the element you need, things go smoothly; if it presses on your weak spot, slow down.
muc.vi_du: The year 2027 is Ding Wei: the stem Ding (Fire), the branch Wei (Earth).

muc.de_hieu: A school that looks at the nine flying stars over time (20-year Periods, years, months) laid over the facing of the house. It is used mostly to choose when to renovate or break ground, and which side to leave undisturbed.

A way of linking each line of a hexagram to an Earthly Branch (Zi, Chou, Yin…) according to its lower and upper trigrams. Through the branch, each line gets an element, so you can work out its Six Relations and compare it with the day and month of casting a hexagram.
muc.vi_du: The Kan hexagram (Water doubled): lines 1 to 6 are Yin, Chen, Wu, Shen, Xu and Zi in turn.

muc.de_hieu: The hexagram you get by changing all six lines: yin becomes yang and yang becomes yin — the opposite side of the situation.
muc.vi_du: The opposite hexagram of Kan (Water doubled) is Li (Fire doubled).

muc.de_hieu: The hexagram you get by turning the six lines upside down (line 6 becomes line 1) — the same matter seen from the other person's side.
muc.vi_du: The inverted hexagram of Zhun (Water over Thunder) is Meng (Mountain over Water).

muc.de_hieu: A way of sorting the 64 hexagrams into 8 groups headed by the 8 pure hexagrams (Qian, Kan, Gen, Zhen, Xun, Li, Kun, Dui). The element of each palace is used to work out the Six Relations of each line, and each hexagram has one Self line and one Response line.
